through_lines.1: By the end, the reader knows that an ordinary village lives inside a Paramāra king's town, whose remains, records and memories all reach back to one eleventh-century act of naming, and that the evidence leaves open whether that act founded the place or took it over.
through_lines.2: By the end, the reader knows the land the founder found: a country with no river at its door and no dependable groundwater, one wet season, black soil and a hill of building stone, so that its water had to be made and its town was built of its own rock. The land is the setting, never the cause.
through_lines.3: By the end, the reader knows that Udaypur's hill stood in an old, named country whose centre, roads and carved shrines lay elsewhere and reached the hill only through proposals, and that by the tenth century its own range had become a crowded frontier.
